newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's forest industry faces another tough year.
newsitem.headline: Canada's forest industry faces another tough year.

text.p: Canada's pulp and paper industry faces another tough year in 1997, with overall profits seen dropping by 25 percent after an estimated 75 percent decline this year.

Canada's publicly held forest products companies are expected to earn about C$1.1 billion ($825 million) in 1997, down from an estimated C$1.5 billion in 1996, Mike MacCallum of Price Waterhouse said after an industry conference hosted by firm on Tuesday.
In 1995, the Canadian pulp and paper industry earned C$5.8 billion.

Canada's newsprint sector, which is expected to earn about C$700 million overall in 1996, will be the hardest hit next year, hurt by a freefall in newsprint prices and a discouraging outlook for consumption in North America, MacCallum said.
"Newsprint will go into a loss position in 1997," he said.

MacCallum expects the Canadian woodpulp sector to break even in 1997, after losing an estimated C$500 million this year. Profits for market segments such as other papers and paperboards and lumber will be comparable to those made in 1996.
MacCallum's analysis was echoed by some of the corporate executives attending the one-day conference on price volatility in the forest products sector.

Paul Planet, vice president of marketing at Abitibi-Price Inc. of Toronto, which has the capacity to make 1.8 million tonnes of newsprint annually, said the newsprint sector is vulnerable to shrinking North American demand.
"There is going to be a hostile market for newsprint by the year 2000," Planet told the gathering.

Although global demand for newsprint is expected to grow by 6.8 percent between 1995 and 1999, mainly because of significantly higher usage in non-Japan Asia, it is expected to shrink by about 0.2 percent in North America, Planet said.

Demand for newsprint in the United States and Canada is being crimped by competing technologies and media that do not use newsprint, and by conservation measures implemented by newspaper publishers whose profits are squeezed.

Yet as North American demand falls, producers worldwide are adding to production capacity. World newsprint output capacity is expected to grow by 7.2 percent to 41 million tonnes by 1999, Planet said.

That apparent imbalance between supply and demand will do little to reduce the increasing volatility of newsprint prices, which in the eastern United States, are currently about $240 below the peak of $765 a tonne reached in the third quarter of 1995.
Between 1990 and 1995, the average year-over-year change in direction of newsprint prices was 15 percent, more than double the average swing of six percent between 1981 and 1985.
The extreme price volatility makes it difficult for both producers and their direct and indirect customers to plan ahead.

As a result, some newsprint producers have expanded too quickly, prompting a painful consolidation in the North American industry. Traditional newsprint customers, meanwhile, are taking drastic measures to deal with wildly fluctuating newsprint prices.
"For the consumers, this means that newsprint has become an unreliable media to advertise in," noted Planet.
